utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. If I may interpose for a moment. Mr. President, you are aware of a matter I communicated to you yesterday. I have confirmed that for our deceased teammate, the memorial service is to be held at 10.30 tomorrow morning, and we would very much appreciate it if the Court could reschedule business tomorrow to facilitate our attendance at that service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me convey to you the Court's condolences. We are very saddened by what happened. In principle, if the Defence counsel are agreeable, we would reschedule the hearing so as to hold it tomorrow afternoon, but we will have to check whether there are any problems. Can we say that we will let you know later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we will hold no hearing tomorrow morning in any case, but let us try and see whether we could, say, for instance, sit from 1.30 to 6.00 tomorrow afternoon, if there's no objection from Defence counsel. All right. We will come back to this matter later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Much appreciated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I just wanted to state to you that the Defence agrees with what the Prosecutor says, and we have no objections whatsoever. Let us reorganise our schedule accordingly. I also wish to avail myself of this opportunity to express the condolences of the Defence to our colleagues, the Prosecutors, on this sad occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. All right. Today, I suggest that we take a break at a quarter past ten. The 30-minute break will be taken at a quarter past ten to reconvene at a quarter to eleven. Let us move on, and I think Counsel Slokovic-Glumac was re-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Re-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Grebenar. You just said during your cross-examination that you heard later on that on the 16th Redzo was killed, I don't know if that is that person's name or nickname, and that this was a person from Prnjavor. Do you know where he was killed or do you know anything else regarding the circumstances of his death?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is true I said that Redzo was killed. That is his name and, believe me, I do not know his last name. I heard about this about a year ago, that on the 16th, a Muslim was killed in Poculica. He was killed somewhere around the school, as far as I heard, but under which circumstances and how, that, I do not know. This person Redzo lived in Prnjavor, but he was killed in this area around the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you personally did not see a thing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: No, no, no. I even think that he was killed after I was wounded. It was in the early evening hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, you mentioned the village of Gornja Dubravica. That is a village which is just below Poculica. You showed it on the map.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Croat houses were there? Could you just tell us that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: Well, Gornja Dubravica spreads out from the road that leads to Sivrino Selo, so perhaps -- I don't know. I don't know the exact number, but there might have been about 50 to 60 Croat houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether these people were informed about the events that would ensue on the 16th in any way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: I think they were not because when we sent the civilians towards Krizancevo Selo, the civilians from Dubravica, Gornja Dubravica, were also by the creek, and together with the civilians from Poculica, they escaped towards Krizancevo Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Croats from Gornja Dubravica fled on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to Kuber, which was relatively close to your village, however, near your village is only one part of Kuber, that is to say, the Vitez side; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: Yes. When one says "Kuber," one means a range of elevations, hills, as we call them, so we had this observation point closer to our village, closer to Poculica, whereas on the other side, the Busovaca side, there was another observation point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't go there, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: No, no, only during the conflict. In 1993, I was there once, and I saw where it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the events in Kuber on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: Well, from the 15th of April, 1993 -- as a matter of fact, later on, I found out a few things. People were retelling what had happened, and during that night, there were some of my people there who were out there on guard duty, and we had said that that night did not differ from any other night, we thought so. During the night, one could hear bits of shooting from Vitez, Tolovici, Vrhovine, but we always thought that, in most cases, fortunately, somebody was just in a very good mood. After a few glasses of beer, perhaps they would pick up a rifle and shoot a burst of gunfire or two. But my group that was out there on the 15th, they realised that from Kuber, from Vrhovine, they could hear some shooting, but only later we found out that -- rather, when I was at the hospital later, I found out that on the Busovaca side where the observation point was for the young men from Busovaca, there was an attack there, and if I remember, they mentioned two or three men being killed during that night between the 15th and 16th of April. That is on the Busovaca side. But here on our side, I heard that there was sporadic shooting, but I really don't know whether there were people who were killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I have finished with this part, but with the permission of the Trial Chamber, I would like to put another question which is not a real question, I mean, one that belongs to cross-examination. It is not really a subject that pertains to cross-examination; however, Zoran Kupreskic said that I interrupted the witness at one point when he started talking about Majda Sivro. So with your permission, I would just like to put one question in addition to what the witness already said, so "Who was Majda Sivro?" Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Majda Sivro and how did Zoran Kupreskic help her?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: Majda Sivro is a Muslim woman. I know her as a co-worker. She was also employed at the SPS factory, and I personally knew her through the obligations we had at work, so that is where we communicated. But Zoran Kupreskic had known Majda from earlier on because I think that Majda's husband, I think his name is Bahtija, was for a certain period of time the president of our or, rather, their cultural society in Vitez. That's where Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic were active. So they were friends with Majda in that respect too. They performed quite a bit outside the borders of Bosnia, and Majda, as the wife of the president, would travel with them on these tours, and that is how they become friends. As regards assistance, yes, I was interrupted yesterday, but I did mention that as soon as the conflict broke out, Zoran asked me when he saw me, he said that he would be embarrassed to show up on his own but he heard that Majda was in her apartment with her children still, and he asked me whether I would be willing to come along with him and to see how she was and whether anything could be done for her, whether she could be helped in any way, because the fact remains that fear prevailed at that time in Vitez and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was at the beginning of the war, is that correct, after the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, after the conflict broke out, five or six days, perhaps, after the conflict broke out. I cannot tell you exactly, but it was at the beginning of the conflict. We went to Majda's apartment. We knocked at the door. Zoran introduced himself because she had asked who it was, and he introduced himself, and he said, "This is Zoran, Majda. Are you in?" And she said, "Yes," and she opened the door and she hugged Zoran and burst into tears, and she said, "What's going on?" And he said, "I have no idea. I imagine everything will turn out fine." I think that he had heard from another lady, a Croat who had worked together with us at the company, I can't remember her exact name, and she asked us whether we'd like to come in and sit down. It was a bit embarrassing, but we did walk in, and we sat down at the dining table. As far as I remember, the children were there too. I'm not sure of the little girl, but, yes, her little children were there with her. And we talked about 10 or 15 minutes. Zoran and her talked a great deal more because they were very friendly, and she asked me about my wounds and whether all my people were still alive and whether I had anything left in Poculica, but Zoran, among other things, asked her whether he could help her in any way, whether she had enough food and other things, and she said that she did for the time being, that she had enough food supplies, but that she was afraid that there were refugees coming in, and the name on the door is a Muslim name, her husband's surname and her surname. She was afraid that perhaps somebody might break-in in the evening or something like that. At that moment, Zoran took me by surprise. He suggested something which I did not approve of then, but it turned out to be the right thing. Actually, he offered Majda to write something down on a piece of paper. What was the rule at that time? When refugees would come in and get into other people's apartments, abandoned apartments, they would just take a little piece of paper and put their name on the door so people would know that this was a Croat and that they wouldn't bang at the door and whatever. Zoran offered that he writes his name on the door, "Zoran Kupreskic," showing that he lived there, and that would protect her, at least to a certain extent. She was truly surprised too by his gesture, and she said, "Well, you are putting yourself in danger too," and he said, "Well, don't worry. I will drop in or Greba --" "Greba" is my nickname, "either he will drop in or I will drop in. Everything will be just fine." Later on I saw Majda once again. I did not go to see her at the apartment, but I know that Zoran went and took her food supplies as well as long as Majda was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have concluded with the redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, of course, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, you are aware that in allowing you to raise a matter in re-examination, which had not been discussed or raised before, we have slightly departed from our basic Rules of Procedure. I thought, however, that this was necessary in the interest of justice. However, we have to stick with some principles, not only the question of a fair trial at the interest of justice, namely, the interest to search for the truth, but also we have to comply with the principle of equality of arms. So therefore it is, I think, appropriate for me to ask the Prosecutor whether they want to ask any question on this particular matter just raised by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Actually, I would have one question to put to the witness regarding this protection that Mr. Zoran Kupreskic granted to his Muslim friend. Re-cross-examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Grebenar tell us why this person of Muslim faith was threatened, why she was in danger, and then, secondly, could he tell us why it was dangerous for Zoran Kupreskic to grant this woman his protection? In what measure is that a heroic act or a brave act from his part? These are the two questions I would like to put to Mr. Grebenar.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the first question was why she felt imperilled, Mrs. Majda Sivro. And I think that is quite clear. If I felt threatened as a man and terrified in my own home in Poculica on that first day, when I was surrounded by Muslims, and when she saw that Croat refugees were coming to Vitez, peoples whose houses were burnt down and who had some of their next of kin killed, of course the woman was afraid. She was afraid that some of these Croat refugees who were flooding into Vitez from all sides could do something out of revolt or revenge. They were all afraid. So may I also answer your other question. In what sense -- I don't know how I should put this. How Mr. Zoran Kupreskic felt. Perhaps the situation was not all that dangerous, but, as you said, it certainly was a brave act on the part of Mr. Kupreskic at that time. Because during the culmination of the conflict, when Croats are being killed on one side and persecuted, to help Muslims on the other side, and to have Muslims helping Croats in Zenica or elsewhere, helping their friends. On the one side there were the Croats and the other side there were the Muslims. It was not considered to be a natural thing, and it could have caused certain incidents. That is why I said that I myself did not approve of Zoran's offer to put up his own name on that door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I put one other question to the witness. Thank you. Mr. Grebenar, are you aware of the fact that Mr. Zoran Kupreskic has granted the same kind of protection to Muslims from the village of Ahmici? Do you know of such cases?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: You mean on the day of the conflict or before that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I am thinking about Zoran Kupreskic's neighbours in Ahmici, whatever the time I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR
utterances.text: I think that Zoran did help them. I cannot speak of that very day, of the outbreak of the conflict. I wasn't there. So I cannot speak of that day. But before that we had quite a few colleagues at work from Ahmici. I think that 70 per cent of the people of Ahmici, either Croats or Muslims, were employed at the SPS factory in Vitez, that is to say, these were our co-workers, we knew them from sight, at least, and also they were his neighbours and his friends more than mine. But I know that in various ways if he could and to the extent he could, he would help people. Zoran Kupreskic was actually head of one section of maintenance at the factory, and he had young men from Ahmici employed there, Muslims, for example. I remember Nermin Ahmic, I think that was his name. I know that once even the head locksmith objected to Zoran and said that he did too many favours to Nermin Ahmic. I mean favours. He allowed him to stay away from work and he took it as part of his annual leave. However, Zoran was familiar with his situation. He had a mother who was ill or something like that and he often had to go to the hospital. So he tried to help this person. He actually explained to Mr. Ahmic's immediate superior that the man was in a difficult situation, that he needed to be helped. He did not only help him on that day, he helped them earlier on. He helped whoever he could help and whoever he had an opportunity to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, I think you are entitled to briefly re-examine, very briefly re-examine, the witness on this very point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we have no questions for the witness. Mr. Grebenar, thank you so much for coming here to testify in Court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, sir. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we move onto our next witness, let me first of all ask Counsel Slokovic-Glumac whether it is -- there's a number 2 on our list, and he is being called by, I think, Counsel Susak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The next witness is Zeljka Rajic. I don't know what number she is listed under.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Number three. She's -- I don't know -- she is a she? She's being called by you and Counsel Radovic. Any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If you don't mind, before we now call the next witness, let me express to you the worries and concerns of the Court about the list of witnesses we received from the Defence counsel. Actually, now we have 111 witnesses to be called by Defence counsel, plus, of course, at least three accused and a few Court witnesses. That amounts to about 120 witnesses. Judging from the pace of our proceedings, this would take about 90 working days, 90 to 95 working days. That means that since we can't sit on Kupreskic every week for the next few months, that we would end probably in July or September only with the Defence case. And then we need, of course, to write our judgment. So I fear that the end -- we are going to put off the end of this trial to the Greek kalends, ad calendas graecas, and, as you know, the Greeks didn't have any kalends. So that means sine die. I wonder whether we could take some steps so as to shorten the list of witnesses. We would like first of all to suggest that as for the 16 character witnesses Defence counsel propose to call, we should apply Rule 94 ter. So we would like to suggest that each Defence counsel intending to call character witnesses should only call one, and for the other ones should provide affidavits, of course subject to any possible objection by the Prosecution. If there are any objection by the Prosecution, of course, the character witnesses will be called here to appear in Court. Now, similarly, as for the four expert witnesses now listed in this document, we would like to apply, again, Rule 94 bis. I assume you have already envisaged this possibility by providing the witness statements of the expert witnesses. I hope so. That means that the -- it is now for the Prosecution to see whether they have any objection. In this way we would reduce by 20, probably, the list of witnesses. In addition we would like to point out that we will not admit any testimony which is repetitive, in particular on Count 1. So please make sure that the future witnesses do not repeat matters or insist on matters which we have already heard. I wonder whether there are any suggestions from either Defence or the Prosecution to the effect that we should try to shorten our proceedings as much as possible, however, because, without saying, that we will never curtail the rights of the Defence. It goes without saying. No suggestion? Let us think it over. Actually, one final question to Counsel Krajina. I assume that the list here submitted includes the three witnesses to be summoned by the Court? Originally there were four. Now you are going to call, through us, only three?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Also make an effort, for instance, remember, we intend to call the anthropologist, an expert witness, and I wonder whether we could simply admit into evidence her book which you have read. I wonder whether you could consider this matter. If you have no objections. You have objections? Yes. All right. So we will call her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are the objections? We really must speed these proceedings up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the expert witness, the anthropologist, I think she has to appear before the Trial Chamber. She needs to respond to several questions which bring into question her whole theory. The theory is, in fact, states that neighbours who were in good relations at one point in time could turn around their lives. In applying this thesis on Ahmici, she would need to respond. How does she know that the crimes in Ahmici were committed by neighbours? If she does not know this, then her thesis that neighbours in Ahmici could have committed this becomes -- it doesn't stand. It only remains on the surface of what she's claiming. So if her book is being used, we insist that she appear before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as regards this anthropologist we just mentioned, I don't think it is proper to ask her to give her opinion on what happened in Ahmici. She doesn't know a thing about what happened in Ahmici, and she cannot give an opinion on these particular events. Now, as for the village itself, she spent some time in the village and she has observed a number of things, so she can give us some explanations. Then it will be your task, Your Honours, to see if what happened in the other villages of the Kiseljak area can, in a way, in certain measure, explain what happened in Ahmici. But that is a decision for you to make. You are also entitled to put questions to that witness about what happened in Ahmici. So I think it is not really possible to just ask that the book she wrote, and which was published by the Princeton University, be admitted in the case file. This, and also the video which she made for the BBC channel. Now, as to the issue you raised earlier and as regards character witnesses. What I would like to stress is that, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, there is no doubt as to the character of the witnesses. We are not aiming to prove before this Court that the accused before the conflict were horrible human beings who had terrifying relations with their Muslim neighbours. I think the contrary is true, and we are not contesting that particular point. So if the Defence are trying to prove that the accused were good neighbours and good human beings, I think indeed Rule 94 ter could be relied upon. We will not contest that point of the Defence strategy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I do share the Prosecutor's opinion. I read the book written by the anthropologist and, as far as I am concerned, there is not one word concerning Ahmici in that book. There is not one word about the crimes committed in that village. So what we need to do is ask the witness to tell us what was the nature of the relationship that existed between the different ethnic groups. Couldn't you give us a general picture of what the situation was? I don't know. What is your position? I am turning towards all the Defence counsels. Now, as far as character witnesses, we've just heard from the Prosecution that they have no objection to the fact that affidavits could be used, in which case I am inviting the Defence counsels to give us that kind of statement and to try to reduce the number of character witnesses to one per accused. One person could come and testify about the character of the witnesses. Mr. Radovic, I see you would like to take the floor. No? Yes, Counsel Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If you permit me, Mr. President, I think the question is not clarified about the expert testimony. As far as I understood, the Court proposes that we get the statements by the expert witness and then the Prosecution would express its opinion. So I would like my learned colleague, Mr. Terrier, to tell us what his position is about that. We have sent the findings to the Prosecution, so we would like to hear the position of the Prosecution regarding the need to bring these expert witnesses before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. As I say, we intend to apply Rule 94 bis. I wonder whether the Prosecutor is ready now to give an answer to say whether they object, they oppose the statements of the expert witness which I've already been provided. If, of course, the Prosecutor needs some time, we can come back to this matter maybe on Friday. Do you need some time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, please. Your Honour, can I just add one thing. As far as our future work is concerned, we would like to be advised well in advance of the change that may interfere in the order of witnesses who will come before you, because of course this will effect our strategy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it's obvious. I think this is what the Prosecution did when calling its own witnesses. The Prosecution warned the Defence well in advance of the changes that took place. So the Defence counsel should behave in the same way and should abide by this principle, very reasonable principle, and a principle which serves the interest of justice. Mr. Terrier, I think by Friday morning you will be able to give us the Prosecution's opinion about what should be done with expert witnesses. So that's settled. I think we can now have the next witness brought in. I think the name of the witness is Mrs. Zeljka Rajic. She can be brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam. I would like to ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may be seated. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Rajic. Could you please tell us where you were born and when and what your occupation is.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: My name is Zeljka Rajic. I was born in Zenica. I lived in Zenica until '75, when I got married, and went to Lasva until '93. That's where I was. Right now I am living in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in 1958.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that until you got married you lived in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you got married, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I went to Lasva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You married Zvonko Rajic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is the village of Lasva, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: The village of Lasva is 18 kilometres away from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It will be easier if you could see the map. Would the usher please show the Court Chamber and the witness this map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked D61/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please indicate where the village of Lasva is, please.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's right here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we see this on the ELMO, please. Could you indicate it now, please, on the ELMO. On this side, Ms. Rajic. Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Zenica is here. So it could be right here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how far is it from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Eighteen kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean Lasva and Busovaca. What's the distance between them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, 17 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Lasva-Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Lasva-Vitez (French translation).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- between French and English translations (French translation). No, there is no difference. Sometimes we hear the French and sometimes we hear the English coming in. (French translation) We have the English translation on channel 4 and the French on channel 5, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: French, not the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that Lasva is between Zenica, Vitez and Busovaca. You will also in the course of your testimony mention another place?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That place is called Dusina?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you tell where Dusina is located on this map. Is the distance between Lasva and Dusina three kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I explain this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Dusina in the direction of Zenica or Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: It's in the direction of Busovaca. It's three kilometres away, but on the map it's kind of difficult to find one's way around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see Busovaca, but I don't know what the black markings mean, but three kilometres would mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, can you help the witness as to where this is pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This is Dusina. This is how I pointed it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So between Zenica and Busovaca, Lasva is halfway on the road?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big was Lasva before the conflict broke out, so in '92?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, how many -- what the Croat population was and what the Muslim population was, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, there were about 500 Muslim houses, that's how many houses they had, and we had 42 of our houses, Croat houses, including Dusina and Lasva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Croat houses were there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Forty-six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Croats lived there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: About 70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about Lasva now.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Lasva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you live with at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: With my husband and three children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were your children?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: My oldest daughter was 16, the younger daughter was 15, and my son was 9 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your husband, Zvonko Rajic, how old was he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: He was 38 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your husband's occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: He was a transporter. He had a transport company. He had his own bus. That's what we call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he had his own bus, a truck, so he was a transporter?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a commander of the HVO in Lasva?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many soldiers were under his command?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: About 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were men from Lasva and Dusina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the first problems between Muslims and Croats in the area of Lasva start?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, these were not problems. First of all, we lost our trust in them because they attacked a village, Bozici, which was three kilometres away from Lasva. It was on a slope, on an elevation, because the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So whose village was this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: This was a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And its name?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Its name was Bozici. There were about 10 of their houses there. In '92, in October, they surrendered their weapons voluntarily because they wanted to move out, but after that, in November of '92, the BH army surrounded the village of Bozici. My husband was fixing his truck, so I was there with him. I was helping him. The phone rang. A young man, one of our young men was up there with a friend of his, visiting a friend of his, and he said, "Bozici has been surrounded." My husband left what he was doing immediately. He looked to see if he could see their village from our house. A group of about 50 soldiers of the BH army had surrounded a part of the forest, there's a forest there, and that's how they were going into their village. My husband took a car, he was all dirty, and he went to that village because he knew they didn't have any weapons, that there was no need for them to go up there. So by the time he arrived, the BH army had separated the men, the husbands, into a barn and were practically beating one by one with iron rods, also wooden rods, so these were like batons. There was also a pregnant woman. They killed her and her husband. My Zvonko, when he got there, since one of the locals from Lasva, a Muslim, was there, he asked him, "Why are you doing this? I would like to see your orders. Where do you get the right to beat people?" I will name this person. This was Batan Pasalic. He told my husband Zvonko, "Don't interfere or the same will happen to you." My husband, of course, had no idea about this. He said, "Let these people go." They didn't let them go. Then they took the women, made them drink oil, and there was quarrelling, but by the time he got there, there was no more shooting, so he rescued those people. One of the men died from the beating, and then after two or three days, these people had left that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Serbs did you say were in the village of Bozici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: About 10 homes, so it's about 20 people. All the youth had left, they went to other towns, so only the older people remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your husband went to help the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the main reason he went there was to warn the BH army soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To warn them that the people in the village were not armed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. All of those people knew, particularly that local Batan villager, he knew that they didn't have any weapons, because Jovica, the Serb, had taken all the weapons to the local community, at the school, and he said Croats and Muslims can be distributed with weapons. So these people had no arms, no weapons at all. This was in October. Then in November, they were attacked and beaten. My husband protected those people practically because they didn't have any ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in November, the village was vacated?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The three people were buried at that time, I was present, and then on that day or two or three days later, everybody moved out from that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a person was your husband?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: My husband was a good man. He was a peaceful man. He helped everybody whenever they had any kind of trouble, any kind of trouble. I think a man like that will not be born again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, nothing happened in Lasva until the 25th of January of '93?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before that, things went on as usual. Our neighbours, women neighbours, Muslims, would come, and they would ask my husband, they're hungry, they have nothing to eat, and they would ask him to go get flour. So he took his truck, and he brought back about 10 tonnes of flour, oil, so that they could survive because we were a minority, and we had what he needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a well-off family?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: That's right. We were practically the richest family. We were rich. My husband struggled throughout his life, but he had everything and he loved people. But after that, on the 25th, an order arrived that we are going to be attacked by the Muslims. I was very scared and a couple of our neighbours too. I wanted to go to Dusina and then move to Busovaca, and I asked my husband to let me go because five women were going and six children and one man. He said, "No, you won't go. Nothing will happen. These are just fantasies." I asked him, I kept asking him until about 2.00, and other people tried to convince him. They said, "Let her go." He had his best man, he was telling him, "Let him go with my wife, and if nothing happens, they'll be back. This is not far." At about 2.00, me and my daughter, my 15-year-old daughter --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 25th. We started off towards Dusina. We went as a group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who was with you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: My daughter was with me, also my sister-in-law and her daughter. That's when we left, but then before us, a man and a woman left. They were older people. In the second group, a woman also -- two women and four children went. They went in twos, so that's about it. So that's how we left Lasva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So mainly women and children?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, mainly women and children, and then that one man who went with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the men remained in Dusina --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, in Lasva. They all remained in Lasva. Only three of us women and four children left Lasva. No one else from the Croat population wanted to leave. They didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I went to Dusina and I arrived in Dusina. It was about half past three when we arrived. The weather was terrible, rainy, windy --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any snow?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a little snow, so we couldn't go to Busovaca. And then we thought, well, we'll just stay here, spend the night here, and we'll leave in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night, in whose house?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: At Ivica Kegelj's, that is his house. There were about 30 of us there altogether. The locals from Dusina also wanted to go to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They had also received some information that the Muslims might attack?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These 30-odd people that were staying at the house, were they civilians, soldiers? Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: As far as soldiers are concerned, there were only two or three of them because there weren't any young people there at all. Practically all of us were civilians. All of us were civilians practically, that is to say, 25 civilians were in the house, and the young men of 18 or 20, there were about five of them, and they belonged to the army. So we spent the night there, and at 5.00 a.m., we got up and sat at the table in order to take our coffee, and all of a sudden an RPG hit the house. We panicked. We didn't know what was going on, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt? What's an RPG?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: It's a rocket launcher. It's for shelling.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Did he ask me that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please explain to the Judge what that is.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Oh, that's a shell, a Zolja. That's what we call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain it to him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I know that it makes a terrible hole in the wall. It was dreadful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a hand-held rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. I'm not very knowledgable in these military matters, but, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the morning, you heard something hit the house; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and then I went to wake up my child. I didn't want my child to be terrified, and I said, "Get up, dear. There seems to be some shooting here." So we all got up and went to the basement of that house, and as we were descending into the basement, we heard cries of "Allah-u-ekber," and I went back immediately and called my husband, and I told him that we were surrounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is "Allah-u-ekber"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It's a word of their's, "Allah-u-ekber." I don't know what it means. I just know that that is what they were shouting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you went to the basement, and then you called your husband; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and I was at the door, and I already saw that some people were killed. A young man had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of this young man who you saw in front of the house?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Drazan, Drazan Kegelj. I called my husband, my husband was asleep, and I said, "Zvonko, Dusina is in flames. We've been surrounded." And he said, "Who? What?" And I said, "They're shouting Allah-u-ekber," and he said, "All right. I'll come up there." So I went back, and as soon as I closed the door, again, one of these shells hit the house. We were crying, we were screaming, actually, and five minutes later, perhaps, we saw people in white with green berets and green bands around their heads, and they had clothing on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean "clothing"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, there was snow, so they were wearing white clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these white uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, like white uniforms. We saw them shooting and hollering, and we opened the door of the basement, and we were crying, of course, and one of us, a man, Stipo Kegelj, went out and said, "Don't kill us. We're surrendering." And they simply grabbed us by the shoulders and got all of us out of the house, lined us up by the wall of the house. Everything we had, anything, rosaries, as we call them, you know, whatever we had of that nature, they tore it off, and also whoever was wearing a cross, they would throw the cross down, and then they would trample all over it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rosaries too? And where were these rosaries?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did have rosaries. Some people wore them around their necks, and others, elderly women, held them in their hands and were praying. Then one of the men said, "We should kill everyone over here."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Rajic. How many people did you see there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: You mean Muslims?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I mean Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Oh, there were a great many of them because there were two groups. First, there was one group that spoke our language, there must have been 50 of them, and there was this other group, they had beards, and they stood away from them, and they didn't move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all of them in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, all of them were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see some of the local Muslims among them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Only one. When he took us to the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a second. Wait a second. Please don't go ahead of your story. You said that you saw a group of Muslim soldiers who were with you, another Muslim group stood a bit further away. Did these people have any kind of insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, "BiH army," yes, yes, on that green or, rather, on that white -- they had a green band saying "Armija BH," BiH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What happened when you were searched and when you were lined up by the wall?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: A local man came and he took us through their village with these army men of theirs. I didn't know any of them. So we passed through the village twice, up and down. Marko Rajic was wounded. They didn't give him any kind of first aid or anything. A soldier even kicked him in the very place where he was wounded, and he asked for help but to no avail. At the intersection, Edin Hakanovic selected 20 younger persons as a human shield, and he left the old people at the intersection. My daughter and I were there and quite a few other people and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. A human shield vis-a-vis who?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Vis-a-vis a hill where our people were. My husband had come to that hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they stood behind you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They put you in front?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the hill that is facing you is where your people are?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is where our people are, my husband and about 15 other members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You and your daughter were in this human shield, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This local person, Edin, he had a loudspeaker, and he called out to my husband, and he said, "Come down to negotiate," and he told him to come down there so that they could reach some kind of an agreement. I saw my husband walking down the hill, and they could not have discussed anything because Edin asked for them to go to Lasva for negotiations. My husband refused. He asked for them to go to Zenica. Throughout this period of time, there was terrible shooting in Lasva, so the civilians who remained down there were surrendered, and they took them to the school in Lasva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you are saying now refers to Lasva; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard about that later, that they were shooting in Lasva?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, it's not that I heard it later. I was there in that clearing, and I could see my village, and there was shooting there, terrible shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were taken to this intersection somewhere halfway towards Lasva; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, all of it is flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw your husband going downhill; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he asked for negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The last time he went down, he had a little white flag or something, some kind of a white rag or something in his hands, and he was waving with it, and he was walking down, and then they agreed. They said that the BiH army would send only 20 and that they would leave their ammunition behind, and Zvonko's men should do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were going to Zenica for negotiations; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I saw them leave, and then they returned us to the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you stopped at the point when you were talking about how you were returned to the village, right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the village of Dusina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they taking you to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: They took us again towards the Muslim village. We made about two rounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say the Muslim part of the village?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Muslim part of the village. They mistreated us all along. They said that they would kill all of us. They took us back to a Croat's house, Stipo Kegelj's house. We were there altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who was there, the people who were taken as human shields?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And the elderly, the women and their husbands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of them are Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of them are Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were elderly people, younger people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Children?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in Stipo Kegelj's house?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think up to 10, up to 10 elderly people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about younger people?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Younger, well, three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say a total of 13 persons?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, a total of 13 persons, the elderly and the three who were sitting there with us, because in this house we were sitting in one room and they were sitting in the other room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these other people?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Croats too, except that they separated us. The men, the elderly on one side, and the elderly with the women and children on the other side. So there was a door and we could see everything that was going on. Then a group of Muslims said all sorts of things to us, and they intimidated us and they mistreated us. They said that they came to cleanse this terrain, that they wanted to kill the Croats. Naturally, we bowed our heads. You didn't dare watch. Another one would come and then he would be nice, because they had tours of guard duty of 15 minutes. Some would say, "Have no fear," and then others would come in and say, "They haven't been killed yet." The elderly men were taken out twice in groups of five or six. They beat them, they returned black and blue, bloody. We were terrified. We cried. "What do you need this for? What have we done to you?" That is what an unknown gentleman had said. They asked us to come in to cleanse this terrain so that there would be no Croats left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what they told you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The last time these five men who were taken out, were taken towards Ivica Kegelj's house. They tied Ivica's hands with a wire and Franjo Kristo's hands with a wire too. But these five men walked behind them and by the house. They were killed individually. They were killed by an unidentified man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these people being killed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It is not far away. It's only a minute or two -- a minute or two distance to the other house. It's practically next door. But Ivica Kristo and Franjo Rajic, they put these people into the garage and covered them with straw so no one could see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you are a bit confused with the names?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, I am not confused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ivica Kegelj and Franjo Kristo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. So afterwards they had to move those people away, those people who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they went together. They went together and they had tied their hands behind their backs. Then they killed these five men, and then these two, that's seven, and then they tried to cover up these killed men so that no one could see this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They did this on orders, right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Naturally they did. The soldier who came to take these people out ordered them to go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of the Muslim soldiers ordered this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the BH army soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ordered them to take these bodies to the garage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to leave them there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, to leave them there and to cover them with straw, with hay, so that the blood couldn't be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of these five men who were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us these names.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Vinko Kegelj, Niko Kegelj, Stipo Kegelj. That's three. I can't mention them in the exact order. If you had a list, I could --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said Vinko Kegelj, Niko Kegelj?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Stipo Kegelj?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Jozo Kegelj in this group?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll go back to that later. All right. After that Ivica Kegelj and Franjo Kristo returned to the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Their hands were tied and these Muslims from the BH army said that they would be killed too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, but we don't understand the reason behind so many -- your questions about so many details about alleged massacres or gross misbehaviour by Muslims against the Croats. What is the relevance to our case?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You will see from our Defence that we believe that approximately the whole story and the goriness of this war starts from Dusina. The effect of what happened in Dusina on the surrounding areas was truly enormous. Until then people lived relatively peacefully and there weren't any major problems between Muslims and Croats. However, this story strained relations and indeed brought about major problems and insecurity to this area. That is the first point. The second reason why we insist on this event is the fact that this event influenced people's consciousness in a major way and also their behaviour on the 16th. I am not talking about the accused, I am talking about other persons who were present in the village of Ahmici on the day when the conflict occurred. That event also had an effect on the consciousness of the accused. We wished to explain why they had weapons when information was received about the Muslim attack. Secondly, I also wish to say that the indictment states that in the Lasva River Valley area, from the first conflict on the 20th of October, 1992 and until the war broke out, on the 16th of April, 1993, it is stated all the time that the HVO attacked unarmed Muslim civilians. Also, in the background of the indictment it is stated that these attacks intensified during the month of January, 1993. So we are refuting these counts in the indictment and we claim that there was no attack on the Muslims. We are proving that in the area of the Lasva River Valley there were only attacks of the BH army against Croat civilians. In view of the fact that the Prosecutor has been asserting the contrary without pinpointing specific events, we are providing you with specific events, and we shall also speak about specific persons. In this part the attack in Lasva, Dusina and then Busovaca, it was exclusively an attack by the BH army against Croat civilians, so we assert that these assertions by the Prosecution are not correct, the assertions cited in the indictment by the Prosecution. So we believe that this witness, and the two following witnesses, who will also talk about the same events, are very important for us. The second witness will testify about the villages around Kacuni and about Busovaca, and the third witness will testify about events in Jelinak, Loncari and Putis, based on which the Prosecutor said that these were attacks by the BH army, which is not true. Because we would like to present what happened in these places. And, of course, it's up to this Trial Chamber to decide which evidence you will admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Although we have some doubts about the relevance of the testimony you propose that we should hear, the relevance to Count 1, we are prepared to admit this evidence, I mean the testimony of the various witnesses. However, may I, on behalf of the Court, call up on you to try to be as concise as possible, not to put too many questions regarding minute details. It is sufficient for us to have some general picture of what happened in that area. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened after that, when the people returned to their houses?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: When they returned to the houses, people were afraid. They didn't tell anybody what had happened. Later a man who came to my room, to our room where the women were, and some men, he had a kind of notebook. He was wearing a green beret and a green band. He had the markings of the 7th unit of the BH army. He sat down at a sewing machine. He was talking very coolly, normally, and he called out Augustin Rados.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that man?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one you said who had come in?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. His name is Serif Patkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he called out Augustin Rados, you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: He took him outside, took him to the other house, killed him, then he came back. Then he said, "Well, you see, Zvonko Rajic, he placed his family, his wife somewhere in Croatia, and I have come to kill them." He was saying that he had been to Croatia to receive medical treatment, that he came in '92 to Zenica from Croatia. And he said, "Thank you to Mr. Tudjman for allowing me to kill his people." He was saying this as he was sitting on top of a sewing machine. And this woman, Zdravka Rados, she said, "It's not true that Zvonko sent his wife and children away." His wife is here and his child is here. He asked where. She directed him towards me, where I was sitting. He turned around. We weren't even half a metre apart from one another and he said, "I know your husband very well. Would you like me to describe him?" I looked frightened. Why was he telling me all of this? He said he was wearing a coloured suit, he had a bullet vest, he had a scorpion, and this is all true. I thought that they could see one another on the road, because he had gone for negotiations to Zenica. He said, "I killed him. I fired a whole magazine into his head." I didn't believe him. He was acting so coolly. I bent my head and I started to cry, naturally. He said, "Go upstairs," in this house, Stipo Kegelj's house. I went. My child was crying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before they took you to the first floor, did they take away other people from the house?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vojo Stanisic was taken away, and then before that, his wife was killed too. Everything that he had written in the notebook, he would read out, "Take away outside and kill."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Pero Ljubicic? Was Pero Ljubicic --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Pero Ljubicic, yes, that's one of the persons who I couldn't remember. That's how each one of them was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people did Serif Patkovic take outside of the house?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Three from my room, from the room where I was, three, and then from another room, five, and then specially these two people separately, Ivica and Franjo, who had to cover these bodies up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the bodies of those who were killed after that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, no, we saw them being taken out and being killed. They probably hid them. We heard the shots, we heard the shooting, so we knew what was happening, and these people didn't come back again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when they took you upstairs to the first floor?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: When I was going up the stairs, there was a man dressed in white. He had a beard. He had a big gun. He didn't say anything. The other person who was taking me said, "We won't kill her. She has money. We'll take that away from her," but they will kind of keep me as a dessert. They took away 100.000 German marks from me and 1.000 dollars. They gave me back 270 German marks. He hit me on the head with this money and said that if I told anybody that this was confiscated, they would kill me, and "Of course, it's your turn anyway, so you will be killed." So I went back downstairs in tears. My child was happy that I returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened to Mladen Kegelj?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was stripped naked, and his hands were tied with wire. His ears were cut off. He was taken through the Muslim village. Other things were cut off too, so this man died. He was killed at the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that any houses were being torched in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we saw that when we were leaving. When they received news from Zenica that not a hair on our heads could be harmed, they went mad. They were enraged. They wanted to burn all of us. We could see the canister where they were keeping the gasoline, and they said, "We came here to kill all the Croats in this territory."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the order arrived to stop with the killing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken after that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: After that, at about 6.00, we were taken to the schoolhouse in Lasva, but for two or three times, we remained there. They were afraid. They were debating whether we would be killed here in this band, so it took us an hour or two with these stops to get to the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you go to Lasva, on foot?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, on foot, and we were barefoot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were going from Lasva to Dusina, on foot?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, also on foot, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Lasva, you were placed in the schoolhouse?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and all the civilians who happened to be in Lasva, they were all captured. Old men, women, children, they were all detained. When I was going down the road, one person, Sisic, I know him well, his last name, he asked us, "Where is Tatin now?" That was my husband's nickname. I couldn't believe that he had killed him. I thought maybe he wanted to scare me. And then later when I stopped next to a wall, a young man kept looking at me, and I kept looking back at him out of fear. He approached me. He had a gun. I thought he would kill me. He said, "Don't look at me anymore. I did not kill your husband." And then it became clear to me that this man had killed my husband, Patkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you released?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: It was 2.00 a.m. There was a guard. We went to my uncle's house. The next morning at 8.00, I went to our house. Everything had been taken away, and the money that I had kept, that I had hidden in my chimney, even that was found. This was dead capital but they had taken it all away. Batan Pasalic, who was in Bozici, was driving my husband's car, and I met him when we were going to the schoolhouse in Lasva from Dusina. He was sitting in my husband's car. I thought maybe -- I had no idea that they had killed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your house was looted?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You left Lasva in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I left Lasva for Zenica. My two children were there at my parents' house, so then I was transferred from my parents' house to Cajdras for safety because I was being followed. I noticed a car that was following me, so for my safety, I spent nine days in Cajdras until the funerals were held for those who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you receive information that the body of your husband had been exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: When did I get this message?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "exchanged"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That it had been returned to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: You mean to the hospital in Zenica? Yes, that's when I heard after five or six days that UNPROFOR had come and taken the dead bodies to the morgue in Zenica and that funeral preparations were being made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at a tape now, and at the beginning of this tape, there is a statement by your husband regarding some kind of misunderstanding about the size and the division of the municipality of Lasva?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second part of the tape shows the bodies of those killed, so if you are not able to watch --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I will watch.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The videotape is marked D62/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The transcript, what is the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number of the transcript is D62A/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Now we will look at the tape. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Conflict from Gornji Vakuf has switched to this area of Central Bosnia where the HVO from Busanica, so according to some information from the accords in Geneva, the Travnik province stretches to the River Bosnia. This is not what's on the transcript. We want peace, and we will wait as people wait for a football match to be over, so we will know that it is over and what the final results are. This is what we're waiting for.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. The problem is that the text is quite inaudible. The tape is quite old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Rajic, could you tell us, do you remember when this took place?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know when this was recorded, I wasn't present, but I think this was probably at the end of '92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's obvious that --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this happened in November. Yes, in November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of what your husband said, that he didn't care who the Lasva municipality would be awarded to, he was, first of all, in favour of peace?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a very peace-loving man. He loved everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could we look at the second part of the tape now, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: These are the massacred people from Lasva, and the names are Zvonko Rajic, Franjo Rajic, Stipo Kegelj, Niko Kegelj, Vinko Kegelj, Dragan Kegelj, Pero Ljubicic, Vojo Stanisic, Mladen Kegelj, and Augustin Rados. In attacks by the Muslim aggressor army, they lost their lives in Lasva. May they rest in peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, don't you think we could stop now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen this tape before?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise your husband?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the hole in his chest where they plucked his heart out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at this list that I will give you and tell us whether these people are the people who were killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked D63/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a list of those who were executed, also captured, who are missing, and also those who are wounded. Are the names on that list familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I only know Jozo Kegelj. He's alive. Stipo, where did I see him? Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether these people were killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, could you please tell us whether this information on the ages of Stipo Kegelj, Vojo Stanisic, and Pero Ljubicic is true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were older men.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also please tell us whether, after what happened in Lasva and Dusina on the 26th, any Croats remained living there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, not a single Croat lives in Lasva anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Dusina?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, have any of the Croats returned?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No. At Dusina, the houses are burned down, and in Lasva where I lived and many other people, Muslims moved into these houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mrs. Rajic. I have concluded my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Also, I would like to tender into evidence as Defence Exhibits D62/2, and D63/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection. They are admitted into evidence. I wonder whether Counsel Radovic would like to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Any other cross-examination by any other Defence counsel. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. No one else will examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's for the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution proposes to ask no questions in cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. There will be no --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but you also had document D61/2, the map, and you didn't ask ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like D61/2 to be admitted into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. It is admitted into evidence. So there will be, therefore, no re-examination. The Court has no questions for the witness. I assume there's no objection to the witness being released. Madam, thank you for giving evidence in court. You may now be released. Thank you.
