utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, sir. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So who will be our next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, it will be Jadranka Tolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. She will be examined in chief by you, Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Then could we have a rough idea of the following witnesses? After Mrs. Tolic, it's Mr. Stojak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Those who are on the list, the list that was already provided to the Prosecutors. I think it's going to be Dragan Stojak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Followed by Mario Rajic and Ljuban Grubesic, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, I wish to say that two witnesses have not arrived from Bosnia or, rather, they arrived only last night. Mario Rajic and Stojak are the persons in question. So, therefore, we cannot hear them now, according to the list that we submitted to the Court, but they will be the first tomorrow after Jadranka Tolic. First it's going to be Grubesic, then Stojak, and then Mario Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Tolic. Good morning. Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Susak will examine this witness in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Susak:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tolic, good day to you.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall be putting questions to you, and you are going to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wish to draw your attention to the following: Please pause awhile before you answer because the interpreters are supposed to do their part of the job too. Would you please tell me where you were born and when?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 12th of January, 1961, and I was born in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I am a nurse. I worked in the general hospital in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you speak slower, please? You said that you worked in Zenica. Where?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: In the hospital in the central laboratory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me who your family members are?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I have a husband, Zoran, and I have two sons, Adrijan and Toni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were they born?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: The older one was born in 1981, and the younger one was born in 1986.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we're on this subject, I'm going to ask you about your brother too. You also had a brother, didn't you? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: My brother's name was Tomislav Trogrlic. He was killed as a civilian when he tried to leave Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It was at the end of June, the beginning of July 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was he born?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: He was born on the 21st of June, 1972.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he was killed as he was trying to leave Zenica. Could you please tell me when you found out about this? When did you find out about the fact that he was killed or did you just think he was missing?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: We did not find out about the killing immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us a bit about this.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of April I fled to Busovaca, the military forces took me there and the telephone lines were still on, and I got a message from my mother in Zenica that my brother would try to join me there, because, in Zenica, there was great intolerance. Young people were being persecuted, Croats. My brother tried to get out of Zenica to join me. He left via Cajdras, Vjetrenica and Poculica. He was killed somewhere up there. However, my mother informed me that he was supposed to come, but he never came. Then we were in correspondence. I received letters through the U.N. They would come to Busovaca and bring humanitarian aid to us, and they brought us letters too. There I realised that he was not at home and that he hadn't come to stay with me either. Then I reported him as missing, hoping that the International Red Cross would find him somewhere. However, we did not succeed in this effort. For two or two-and-a-half years we did not know whether he was dead or alive. We found out only in 1996. I heard from a relative of mine who spent the entire war, until 1994, in Cajdras. Some policeman who worked in that part of Zenica came to have a cup of coffee at her place and they asked her who she was and where she was from. When they heard that her last name was Trogrlic, they said that to the best of their knowledge a man called Trogrlic was killed at the end of June, beginning of July, 1993 at Vjetrenica. When the cease-fire was established in '94, she came to Busovaca and she told me about this. Then I started looking for my brother, and I went to Zenica to the International Red Cross, to the Red Cross of the town of Zenica. I asked other people from town to help me find him. When we found out what the exact location was, we agreed on the exhumation, and then his mortal remains were transferred to Split. That is where the exhumation took place. And he was buried in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now we shall go back to other questions, to the very beginning. You said you lived and worked in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the basic structure of Zenica was, tell us very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I shall. There was a census in 1990 and about 11 per cent of the population was Serbs, 17 per cent were Croats, and the rest -- there were two or three per cent who were others, and all the rest were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the relations were between the Muslims and the Croats, what they were like before the conflict and what about after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, before the conflict, when the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina started, the Serb aggression, then the Territorial Defence was organised. Then there was mobilisation of all who were employed. They received their war assignments in the places where they worked and then they were taken to garrisons where the former Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA had been. All the citizens were there together. There were Serbs and Croats and Muslims in that Territorial Defence, I mean. Then it was being said that this would be a joint defence against the aggressors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are referring to the Territorial Defence when you say TO?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am referring to the Territorial Defence of the city of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took part in this Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When were the relations between the Croats and the Muslims aggravated?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: First there were milder forms of aggravation, because they were defending themselves against the Serbs, and the Serbs were attacking from the village of Cekrcici, from some mountain, I think. It was mostly Territorial Defence units that went up there. It was noticed up there and people were saying that Croats were mainly put in the first lines. Then people started dodging the TO, the Territorial Defence. Then the relations worsened even further during the attack in January, 1993. However, there is another thing I have to mention, something that happened earlier. When the Mujahedins came to the town of Zenica, then there was a worsening of relations. Also, when the crime in Dusina took place, and also the attack on Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the Mujahedins. Who are these Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: The Mujahedins were foreign nationals who came to Bosnia-Herzegovina and who behaved differently from our local Muslims. However, they brought along with them certain changes, laws of their own. Until then there was some kind of tolerance. We even got along pretty well with one another. But when the Mujahedins came, they tried to re-educate our Muslims. They tried to change them. Actually, the Mujahedins hated everything that was not Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you, the city people, recognise the Mujahedins? How did you know that you saw them?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I knew when I would see them because they all wore beards. Our local Muslims, citizens of Zenica who had joined them, also started wearing beards, and they wore a special kind of headdress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's how you recognised them?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how we recognised them. The Mujahedins patrolled the streets and they were intimidating the non-Muslim population. They sang different songs. And our people who joined them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Just a minute, Madam. Could you please speak a little bit slower.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time fear prevailed, because they were patrolling the streets and they were marching along the streets and they were singing from Sarajevo to Vranducka Vrata, there will be no Serbs or Croats. They also had other slogans, like this country Bosnia will be Turkish. This was a sign to the non-Muslim population that there would be no life for us there, that there could be no life together. That we would not feel free there, that we will not be able to live and work there as we had until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now you said that you worked in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: From 1981 until 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the relations between the Croats and Muslims like in the hospital itself? I am referring to the physicians employed there.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1991, political debate started about the representatives of the Muslim, Croat and Serb peoples. There were squabbles every day, quarrels. The majority of the population in Zenica was Muslim and also most of the people employed at the hospital were Muslim too. We started feeling threatened among them. That is exactly what they wanted. Because in '92 a large number of expelled Muslims from other parts of Bosnia started coming into Zenica. At work they started telling us that there was no room for the Serbs and Croats there, that they should leave the hospital so that they could find jobs for their refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I help you at this point. Could you please tell us what the reasons are, why you left the Zenica hospital?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am going to tell you my reasons. One of my bosses, the second one in line, would often invite me to her office. She would debate various points with me and would often ask me how I could be a Croat, because I was born in Bosnia. It wasn't only once. Twice a week or once a week she would call me in for such interrogations and she would ask for an answer. I also had other unpleasant situations in the laboratory. We wore white uniforms and then when they got dirty we would send them out for washing. Then they were sent back and there were crosses on our sleeves or on our pockets. That was a sign that was supposed to show who the non-Muslim workers were. And that offended me terribly. Then there were these other interrogations, and they said we had drawn this ourselves. We couldn't even work and breathe in the hospital normally, let alone do something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any other similar incidents in the hospital, especially how were the Croats treated and how were the Muslims treated? Again, I am talking about the period before the conflict or, rather, before the attack on the 18th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that the Muslims did not conduct themselves well towards non-Muslim wounded who came from the surrounding towns around Zenica. There was fighting in Zepce, Orasje, and so on, Uskoplje. So I think they neglected people. Not so much in that period, but later this became very pronounced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say later, you mean after the 18th. Now, let's go back to the beginning. You mentioned that many things were getting worse after the attack against Busovaca in January. What happened in Zenica the day before the attack in Busovaca? What was the atmosphere in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: The atmosphere at the end of January, in '93, was very tense, but ordinary citizens didn't know what was going on. The town was already in darkness in the early afternoon. It would get dark around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. We had no electricity at night, so the town was dark. So this had a terrible effect. There were armed soldiers in the buildings of Zenica. On any higher building, where they had a good view, there were sniper nests. This was very frightening for us. We didn't know why, against whom. The citizens felt very insecure. There was a kind of calm. You couldn't even talk loudly. We would whisper. We didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Muslims arriving at that town from Busovaca to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Just by coincidence, I was walking in the daytime, I live in Zenica, there are four tall high-rise buildings, so maybe I was going shopping and I was passing by. I saw a truck and there were two vehicles and women and children were coming out of these vehicles. And this was unusual -- this was not unusual to see in Zenica, because expelled persons would arrive from different places every day. This looked very dismal. People were crying. So I asked them where they were from, because people would come, these expelled people would come to the door everyday. They would ask for help in bread or money. So when I saw them, I asked them where they were from. They said from Busovaca. I was surprised. I thought, "What is happening there?" If they arrived -- if expelled persons were coming from Busovaca to Zenica, this was not clear to me. I was confused when I went home, because earlier people were arriving from Potkozarje or Gorazde, but I was very surprised how come these people came from Busovaca because nothing had happened before then. At least we didn't know about anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your experience at the time when the Muslims were arriving to Zenica? Did they visit you in your apartments, did they do anything?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really say anything about that. I don't know about that period, because if somebody did come to the door to ask for bread, I never asked where they were from. I could say for the later period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll talk about that later, because we will discuss the other events after the 18th of April. You said you worked in the hospital. After that, where did you go, after you left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I already told my reasons for leaving the Zenica hospital. I would like to add another reason. This would be instructive. I am a graduate of medical high school and I was a senior lab technician. We had received new computers for blood analysis, and there were about 45 of us. I was among the five chosen to be senior lab technicians to work on these computers. So during these events, in the war, I was removed from this post and I was given the lowest ranking post in the lab. They returned me like a beginner to work on urine analysis. So I left the hospital. For a period I was at home, and then I found out that a kind of medical unit at the crisis committee was being formed where Croat people were gathering. So I reported there to work as a nurse. They accepted me. I started with the establishment of the medical unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this located in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: At the beginning we started in the elementary school, Sestra Dietrich Ditrih. And then because the school year was supposed to start, we had to vacate those premises and then we went to Cajdras to work. We worked in a private house from there that belonged to a Croat who was working abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So now we have finished with the period of your work in the Zenica hospital, and we will move to another question. It's a kind of continuation. When did all these incidents, all these incidents of behaviour, untoward behaviour of Muslims towards Croats, when did the division between Muslims and Croats take place, generally speaking, in the Territorial Defence and in the authorities?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I already said that Croats, Muslims and a small number of Serbs had been part of the TO who had not already left the town, but the division came about when the Muslim politicians -- I don't know how to call them -- when the Muslim people started to form the BH army. They started to form some kind of defence forces. There was the Patriotic League, the Green League, the 7th Muslim, then the Mujahedins founded the MOS, the Muslim defence forces, MOS. So these were all things being formed so that the Muslim people could defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were these several formations?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Then the Croats saw that Muslims were grouping themselves in their national structures. The Croats felt insecure because we were so few in number, and they had already been so many indications that we were not welcome, and that we didn't feel safe. So out of fear Croats started to organise Crisis Staffs. And, depending on the part of the town where there were, perhaps, majority Croat population, this is where these staffs were formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned MOS. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Muslim liberation forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who comprised this organisation?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: The Muslim defence force were comprised mostly of Mujahedins and they were joined by local Muslims. Not all, of course. Mostly they were in the BH army, but a large number of them also joined the Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did MOS operate together with the BH army or separately?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. All the units that were being formed, I would call them altogether by one name, Muslim forces, including the BH army, the Green Legion, the Patriotic Legion, and the MOS, Mujahedin organisation. These were all Muslim forces. They operated together in coordination, and that's how they carried out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the civilian authorities, was there any police in Zenica? Was there military and civilian police?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were two police forces. There was the civilian police of the town of Zenica and there was the military police. When the Crisis Staff of the Croatian people was formed, they started -- also they elected some people who were familiar with these affairs. They were officials in the civilian component, so they came to the Crisis Staffs of the Croatian people at that time. And then they founded the police of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't say anything more about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In view of the fact that you were in Zenica, were there any terrible incidents by Muslims against Croats? For example, were there any rapes?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard of several cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us, two cases?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that Ana Spasojevic, an old lady who was over 60 years old, was in her house, and this was in a village quite high up. She was there with her son, who is mentally retarded. They were alone in the house -- no, her husband was there too. No, her husband was in the hospital at the time. He died shortly afterwards. They were attacked by masked persons. The old woman was raped. Her name was Ana Spasojevic. Then after that she and her son were both tied to the bed until the neighbours found them. And this was done by some masked persons. They had black masks on their heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about another case?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, another case that I heard had happened somewhere in Drivusa. That's the Drivusa settlement. It's a young woman who had two young children. She had been raped in front of her children and her mother and father-in-law. I don't know her name. I heard about both of these cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will move to another question now. You mentioned these incidents before that had happened. What were the reasons for Croats to leave Zenica? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: The reasons why Croats left Zenica were that the life conditions were intolerable, but the main reasons were the attack on Dusina and the crimes in Dusina, and this horrified the citizens, Croats in Zenica, and other citizens. Then the attack on Busovaca. Then from that time Croats in Zenica felt very insecure. They were afraid for their own lives and the lives of their children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about Dusina?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that Dusina is a place before Zenica, when you go from Sarajevo towards Zenica. It's before Zenica. And a major crime was committed there, that 10 or 12 people were killed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think this crime in Dusina was committed?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I never know why people commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then one of the reasons that caused fear among the citizens was because of what happened in Dusina. Was there any fear as a result of the arrest of Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was another case. This happened in Zenica itself. We could see this for ourselves. We could see what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. Did you see that event?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, when it was happening I didn't see it. I came by that road shortly afterwards, because I was on my way to work in Cajdras. So this happened close to my house. So I had to pass by. And I was passing by and I happened to see. I was on my way to work. I didn't know what was going on. But then I came by and I saw the car where our people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anybody among the victims?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that crime, and I will call it a crime, my cousin, Ivica Vidovic, was there, and then two other people that I knew, Tihomir Ljubic and Anto Zrnic, I knew the two of them. There was also Marko Ljubic, but I hadn't seen him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you see the police when you were passing by?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were already there. I think they were from the civilian police of the city of Zenica. They were blocking the road -- people were blocking the road so you couldn't get past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now we'll move onto something else. It's a continuation. Who do you think arrested Zivko Totic and why?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know, I heard from my neighbours, because I lived there. I had a house there. I heard that they saw a minivan and people with beards. These were members of the Muslim armed forces, meaning Mujahedins. They arrested him and they killed Zivko Totic's escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were killed in the escort altogether?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Four were killed from the escort and a passer-by was killed too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Zivko Totic was captured, and you said he was captured by the Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who negotiated for the release of Zivko Totic? Was it MOS or was it the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Who negotiated? Well, I wouldn't know that. But I know when Zivko was exchanged. The negotiations were conducted by members of the BH army and the U.N.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who was exchanged for Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: When he arrived to Vitez and Busovaca, we met in Busovaca and he told me that he was exchanged and some captured Mujahedins were exchanged for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the BH army carried out the negotiations and exchanged Zivko Totic for Mujahedins. What does this tell you?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I said already earlier that these were Muslim forces, and they did everything in coordination. Both the Mujahedin and the BH army, these were not separate structures. The Mujahedin were part of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because the BH army, in fact, representatives of the BH army, sometimes justified themselves by saying that they did not have any tight coordination links with MOS?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: That's not true. They did closely coordinate with them, so MOS, the Mujahedin, would carry out some bad things which the BH army wanted to conceal, and this is how they would make excuses. They would say, "We had nothing to do with this. We cannot do anything," but this wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We have now come to the 18th of April, 1993, and that is to say, the date when the Croats of Zenica were attacked, and we're going to say a few words about that. Where were you on the 17th? On the 17th of April, did you notice anything in the town of Zenica on that day or before that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like to start with the 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. A day or two earlier.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to start with the 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just one more thing, Mr. President. Do you know why the Mujahedin captured Zivko Totic, but then you took me back to the 15th. Do you know? Please tell us now.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: From the 18th until the 15th -- well, I'll tell you my conclusions after the 18th. I think that they arrested him. I think they arrested him for one reason so that the HVO, already at that point, would remain without its main staff, that is to say, that they abducted the key man of the Croat people. We were left without a leader after Zivko was arrested. We didn't know what to do because he was the most knowledgable man amongst us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that already a sign that the Muslims were preparing attack against the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: We did not think so then. We did not know it. On the 15th and all the way up to the 18th, we expected them to return Zivko to us, and that was the only subject of people's conversations, and we had no intimations of the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you say that you will say something about the 15th and the 16th of April, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I shall start with the 15th. Zivko Totic was arrested. His escorts were killed. It was a terrible sight. For us, the Croatian people, it was so discouraging that we did not know what to think. This was proof to us that we certainly could not go on living there, nor could we behave and work freely and normally. There was chaos in the town of Zenica. They arrested Zivko. They killed five men, also a fifth one, an accidental passerby. This had a terrible effect on all the citizens of Zenica, not only Croats, all honest citizens. Chaos prevailed in town. The town was blocked. There were police everywhere. Until then, police patrols were not that frequent. I know. I went to work on the 15th in the morning from Podbrezje to Cajdras. That is where I went to work. We had some kind of a mini clinic there, a mini hospital. I saw what happened. I couldn't pass because the police wouldn't let us pass, and I went back to Trokuce where the HVO headquarters was. They called, from there, the hospital in Cajdras, and they said that they should send an ambulance to pick me up because they found out that only ambulances could drive through town. So it was an ambulance that came to pick me up at Trokuce, and I was taken to Cajdras. They returned me to Trokuce from there too because that is where the Croat headquarters was, the HVO headquarters, and there were several medical persons there. The people who remained, rather, at headquarters wanted to have one medical person there, if need be. Zivko Totic's brother was there, and he didn't feel very well, and that is why they took me back there. So in the morning of the 15th, I took my first aid bag and some medical material, infusions, things like that, things I thought that would be needed just in case, and I returned to the headquarters. This was actually the building of a company called Vatrostana, and that is where the HVO headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now we're going to move on to the 18th of April, to the attack.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: All right. From the 15th to the 18th, I stayed at headquarters. I lived nearby --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Do you mind if we take a break now, a 15-minute break, before you move on to the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the best point of all because I'm moving on to another subject. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall continue my questions. We have already touched upon the 18th of April, 1993. Do you know whether there were any attacks in Zenica on that day?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was. I repeat, the 15th, I went back to headquarters. I was in Podbrezje or, rather, in Trokuce where the headquarters building was, and I stayed there until the 18th. There was chaos. We, the others who were working at headquarters, we just knew that they asked for the unconditional release of Zivko Totic. Obviously, they had not succeeded in this. There was chaos there. I was there to take care of the men at headquarters. For example, Zivko Totic's brother, Zeljko Totic, that was his youngest brother, he was in very bad shape. He needed pills. He needed tranquilisers. On the morning of the 18th -- well, I spent all the night there. From the 15th until the 18th, I was there at headquarters. My home was nearby, and I would only go occasionally to refresh myself. On the 18th in the evening, I was also at headquarters. I was awake until midnight or even after midnight, 1.00. I went to a room where there were mattresses on the floor, and I wanted to get some rest. I fell asleep. In the morning, I heard a shot ring out. It wasn't a shot from a rifle. It was like a grenade or something like that. It was twenty past five in the morning. I jumped up. I put my shoes on, and I realised that there was another military man there, and we went out in front of the building. In front of the building, we were all terrified, frightened. We heard shots from rifles. We were terribly afraid. Then we finally realised that it had started, that that was an attack on headquarters. Around ten to six, they brought a man to me, and they asked me to help him, but I could not help him. He was already dead. His name was Vlado Lovrenovic. He was my neighbour. He was a civilian. He was not a member of the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you a bit? You said that you were in Trokuce, and that's where the headquarters was. Could you please tell me what happened after Trokuce in terms of your movement?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Certainly. The attack started at twenty past five, and we stayed there for awhile because of the shooting, and then we moved out at around 8.30. From Trokuce, we went to a village which is above that area, and that is called Podbrezje. That is where I lived. That is where my home was. Then we went further up, above that village of mine, and that is where they told me that there were some people who were wounded. The headquarters, the members of the main staff and all those who were working there, went ahead, and I had to stay behind and wait for the wounded to come in so that I could help the wounded person, and a few men stayed to help me with him, that is to say, to carry him. His name was Marko Dujic. He was shot in the chest, and I gave him an infusion there. I bandaged his wounds. We tried to catch up with the rest who were ahead of us. We went from Trokuce to Podbrezje and from Podbrezje to Zmajevac. Zmajevac is a hill. We reached that hill around 11.00, 11.30. From there, others took over this wounded man. There was a car there. I think it was a minivan. It was not a proper ambulance. We had to go on foot all the way, the military and the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said "the military and the civilians." Where did you go from Zmajevac?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: From Zmajevac, we went from Grm, and from Grm, we came to Cajdras.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where this place Cajdras is?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Cajdras? Cajdras, there is a road going through Cajdras that links Zenica to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you reached Cajdras, how much time did you spend there? Are we still talking about the 18th?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, we're still talking about the 18th. We could have reached Cajdras around 12.30 or 1.00. I stayed there until 11.00 p.m. There were many civilians there, also the military. There were many people there. Panic prevailed. Children were crying. Old women were passing out. My colleagues and I had a lot of things to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you still in the medical corps?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you were there until 11.00 p.m.? What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: After that, the U.N. forces came in, the joint authorities or the police. There were some negotiations there in a building, in a house across the street from the church, and they asked the military to surrender their weapons unconditionally, to board buses, and then they were taken to the corrections house. Mothers were crying because of their sons and their husbands. Chaos prevailed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all taken to the corrections house or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Those who were in Cajdras were taken to the corrections house of Zenica, and the civilians who were arrested by the MOS in town and in other Croat settlements were taken to the MOS building where the Mujahedin were staying. That was the music school of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is where they put up the women and children?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was there then?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: The Mujahedin arrested civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Civilians?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Civilians. Men, as far as I know, I don't know whether there were any women there, but they took the men to MOS, and they beat them up very badly there. They used wooden sticks, big ones, and rifles and metal bars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the corrections house? Were Croats treated better there or at the music house?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I found out later that they were treated far more cruelly in the music school. When I was released from the house of corrections --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you released from the corrections house? Please answer my questions. Do you know when you were released from the corrections house?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I was released on Tuesday. That was the 20th of April, '93 around 1.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, could the usher please show this paper to the witness? One of the copies goes to the interpreters too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D8/4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tolic, in front of you, you have a decision on custody. Do you see the date? Do you see the date when you were sent to custody?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. "Custody will start on the 18th of April, 1993 at 1 --"

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. There are no copies for the Prosecution, nor for the translators.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUSAK
utterances.text: I did give copies but they were supposed to be grouped properly. Here you are. We have two decisions, one on custody and the other one on release from custody. You even have translations into English of each and every one of these decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive a copy of that decision?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given this decision when you were brought into custody at the corrections house?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: No, I got this decision, as well as the other one, on release from custody, when I was leaving the corrections house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you how you could seek legal assistance and how you could appeal this decision on custody?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not receive any such information?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you why they were taking you into custody?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they know that you were working in the medical corps?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they knew it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now tell me how come they knew?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: They knew because they took me into custody in my white nurse's uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you always wear that white uniform?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they brought you into custody, did you introduce yourself, that you belonged to the medical corps, to that formation?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I introduced myself. When I was brought into custody, I asked to speak to the warden of this prison, and I was taken to him. It was an elderly gentleman. I don't know his name. I asked him why I was there, and he said, "I don't know." And then I said, "Take me to someone who does know," and he gave a rough response or, actually, he addressed the two guards escorting me and said, "Take her away," and they took me to a cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days did you spend in prison?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Two days, from the 18th until the 20th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were released from custody, was everybody else released from custody?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not? Do you know why not? How come you were released before other people?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know the reasons why. Many people stayed. After me, they released other individuals. This was some kind of an unofficial exchange. Some kind of concessions were made. I think, if I may continue, because there were three other persons, three women in the cell, young women, I found out from one of the detainees, as I woke up for two mornings in the cell and I didn't have any personal hygiene items, she offered me her's. Her name was Fatima. She gave me a little bit of toothpaste on my finger. She gave me her soap, and she said that on Tuesday, this was Monday morning, she said, "Tomorrow, the International Red Cross will come probably tomorrow to tour, and then you will get whatever you need." I was released from the corrections house earlier, so thank God I wasn't there for that visit by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's complete the cycle of your movements. When did you leave Zenica and where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I left Zenica when I was released from the house of corrections. I got in touch by telephone with a former work colleague of mine from the Zenica hospital who had left the Zenica hospital and went to work in Busovaca because that's where she was born. I called her on the telephone and asked her for help. I told her that I had been detained and that I was very afraid because I had heard from the other citizens that when you are released from the house of corrections by the BH army, then they usually -- or members of MOS, the Mujahedin, would arrest these people and take them to the music school, so I was very afraid. I explained this to her, and she asked for help in my name in Busovaca, and they called me then and they told me that UNPROFOR will come and pick me up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other way to leave Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Some people offered, they offered for me to leave my apartment and for them to take me towards the direction of Zepce, but by that time I had already talked to my colleague, and they told me from the Busovaca police to remain calm, to be patient for a day or two, and that they will send UNPROFOR to collect me and my family. This is what happened. I refused these other offers to go towards Zepce, because many of my other citizens in Zenica, when they tried to leave Zenica, ugly things had happened. They would take them in the direction of Zepce, Vares and some other exits. I don't know exactly which ones. But they couldn't leave. Some couldn't leave. So they would come back. And then once they came back, their house had already, or apartment, would already be occupied. And such exchanges and departures where people would pay, they would be sent to dangerous places. I know, and I heard about the whole family, Strbac, their case, where the whole family was supposed to be taken out from Zenica to the crossing towards Vitez, but they were sent to mine fields and they all perished. So this was a family, husband, wife and children. I think two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you left the house of correction, you spent some time in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in peace there?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: No. There was no question of peace. It could not have been like that. Arrests were already being carried out and I heard from the other citizens that people were being arrested, people were being taken to the music school and to the house of correction. Also, I had different kinds of provocations. They called me on the phone all day. They would threaten me, call me by insulting names. My children couldn't go out any more. Before, when they played in front of the building, the other children would abuse them. They would hit them. So after that they didn't go out any more. There were constant threats over the telephone, and I kept expecting for somebody to come to my door and to take us away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they know where Croats lived in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, this wasn't difficult to know. They had members of their units in the buildings, not Muslims in the buildings. It would always be people who wanted to -- not all, I have to say not all citizens, not all Muslim citizens were the same, but there were persons who would, during the night, place crosses on the doors of non-Muslim citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did that cross represent?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, that Muslims were not living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: But non-Muslim populations were living there, Croats, Serbs, Jews. There were a few Jews in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now we have finished with your movements. I am going back to the beginning, the 18th of April, there was an attack. Who attacked whom? What you know? Tell us what you know.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim forces attacked the headquarters of the HVO and the surrounding towns with the majority Croat populations. The attack was from the direction of Gradac. This is a place above Trokuce and Podbrezje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this east or west when you look from Zenica, or which side did the attack come from?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you whether it was east or west. I just know that I was in Trokuce. The attack came from the neighbouring town, Gradista. It's a large Muslim settlement. They attacked the command in Trokuca, the village of Podbrezje, Kozarci, Stranjani. This was all linked up, up to Cajdras.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Zmajevac and Janjac?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, Zmajevac, this is a part of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all of these places with majority Croat populations?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the attack of the 18th of April, do you know what was going on with the HOS on the 17th of April, or thereabouts, in '93?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: When I was released from the house of correction on the 20th of April, after that my friends and acquaintances came to see me, to see how I was doing, what had happened to me in the house of correction, was I physically abused. And then I found out from them that the day before the region of Crkvice was disarmed where there was one building where HOS was situated. Then Radakovo, Perin Han, Lukovo Polje, they had a command also in Radakovo. Not a command, a kind of command post. Yes, a command post. So they disarmed them. These places are on the right side of the Bosna River. Then I also heard that they disarmed -- I am talking about the 16th and the 17th. I don't know what happened on what day, but the 16th and the 17th of April I know they disarmed Raspotocje. This is already on the left side of the River Bosna. I also heard then, because this was already the left side, Raspotocje, then we have Gornja Zenica. Above Gornja Zenica we have Kuber. This is where I heard -- so this is the 16th, the 17th, the 15th, when that part or those parts of the town were being disarmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we are not saying that Raspotocje was disarmed on one side of the river. Were all the Croats on the other side of the river disarmed also, in view of all of these places that you had mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I repeat again that I only heard this after the 20th, when I was released, which means that there was disarming going on. Not only in these places, they were also disarming the HOS forces which were also in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understood you, you said they were in the centre of the town and in Radakovo?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: No, in Crkvice, the HOS forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were the HOS forces in Crkvice also disarmed?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time on the same same day?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I know the disarming went on on the 16th and the 17th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Kuber. How far is Kuber away from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Kuber, yes. Kuber is like a big hill. I can't really call it a mountain above Zenica. I don't know how far it is from Zenica. I was never up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I know about a Croatian settlement, Gornja Zenica, where there was a majority Croat population and that's maybe not more than 10 kilometres away from town. Then above that settlement, above Gornja Zenica, Bilovode, Travnik, and so on, Kuber was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about Kuber? Who held Kuber, Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I know that a part of our forces were in Kuber earlier, but I heard that there was an attack up there already on the 15th, and that from the 15th Kuber was held by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the 15th, can you say the date, then the month and the year?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I apologise, the 15th of April. So this was already happening up there when they had already arrested Zivko Totic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this hill of Kuber an important point from a military standpoint?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard this from my patients, from the injured, that this was an important elevation, because you could see the whole of Zenica from that hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the attack started on the 15th of April, 1993. How long did it last? Did you hear that maybe from the wounded or from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it last, this conflict or the attack in Kuber? Was it on the 15th, the 16th, the 17th?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say from what I heard. I heard from the 15th there was some minor battles there, which means that Muslim forces took Kuber on the 15th. Whether there were any battles on the 16th or the 17th, that I don't know. But I know that on the 18th the Muslim forces starting going towards other places from Kuber. And I know that from the events that happened up there. They burnt houses up there. There were a lot of injured people up there. Four bodies were found in that house. One of those bodies was the father of Stipo Kristo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of anybody else being killed up there, among the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but -- I heard people were killed, but I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. So we are finished now with the 18th. Since the attack on Zivko Totic, and then we talked about the 15th in Kuber and then the 18th in Zenica, how did the Muslims and the Muslim authorities behave towards the Croats in Zenica? What period are you talking about? Well, I will repeat that. We talked about the 15th of April and then we finished talking about the 18th of April. So what was the behaviour of the Muslims and their authorities on the 18th and after that towards the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard about that. The situation was terrible. I left on the 18th. So I heard about this while I was in Zenica, for a week maybe after I was released from the house of correction. Arrests were being made, houses were being searched. The MOS forces, the Mujahedins, would be going around the villages that were populated by Croats and they would mistreat civilians and old people. They would enter their houses. They would break and take down holy pictures and crosses. They shot in churches. They destroyed the cemetery. They destroyed about 76 tombstones. And I think they behaved very savagely. After that, I can say something about the events in Sircavica I heard about. They went up there, they went into the church, they abused the priest and the nuns. They tied them and they really mistreated the priest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Muslim authorities take care of civilians? Was there any kind of decision reached on the 18th or after that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: In that period they did not, but I heard later -- I was already out of Zenica --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was talking about what you had heard, not what you had seen.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I wasn't there any more, but later, which means this could already have been May and June of '93, they sent to the village of Podbrezje, U.N. forces to protect the population, but before that, before the U.N. forces arrived, this was the Turkish battalion, there was the civilian police from the town of Zenica which protected the Croat population that remained in the village. But this wasn't enough, because the MOS forces, the Mujahedins, had captured the former headquarters of the HVO and they moved in there. This became their headquarters. So every day, at night and during the day, they would patrol the village. They would make arrests, and they would beat the population there, the men who happened to be in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you left the hospital, did you ever return to the hospital? Did you visit the HVO soldiers in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: This was in the period after I had left the hospital and I was working at the Crisis Staff where the Croat forces were being formed, where the Croat people were grouping themselves. Wounded people were coming from Zepce and Usora and they were fighting against the aggressor together with the Muslims. So all the wounded from those areas would come to the Zenica hospital for treatment and, in view of the fact that there was hunger already, then we would go once or twice a week from the medical unit to visit the wounded from other places. We would take them sandwiches or something like that. Already at that time, and this was the second half of '92 and the beginning of '93, I would go and visit those wounded. And there was some very unpleasant, uncomfortable situations. There were already some wounded Mujahedins there and they would see whom we were visiting and they would show the sign of the cross and make this gesture (indicating). They knew who we were and who these wounded were. So they were showing us what they thought about us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they would show you the sign of the cross?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: This is how they would show us the sign of the cross, because many of them couldn't talk, and then this is what they would show us (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: That we should have our throats cut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Mujahedins come to the hospital armed or did somebody else come in armed?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, when we were coming in to see the wounded, no one was allowed to have weapons. Their colleagues who went to see our wounded had to leave their weapons at the reception desk, at the entrance to the hospital. However, this rule did not apply to the Mujahedins. They entered the hospital armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who walked around the hospital or, rather, who guarded the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: There were always MOS members there and there were also people who worked as guards earlier on at the reception desk. However, MOS members were all around the building and in the building too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what they looked like, these people who walked around the hospital and who guarded it and who came in with weapons?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Most of them had long beards and some of them had some kind of headdress and others didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: They did wear military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people from the BH army, did they see that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Everybody saw that and everybody knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we are going to move onto another subject. Do you know how and when Croats left Zenica? Was Zenica abandoned by the Croats even before the 18th of April, and did people move out after that too?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, people did move out, but I am going to tell you about it now. At the beginning of the war, immediately after the Serb aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, many people who had somewhere to go to did, because they were afraid of the war, and they tried to get out of Zenica, both Muslims and Croats, those who could get out. As I said, some people had money. Other people had friends, acquaintances, relatives. But this was not massive at that stage. However, after the 15th of April, and after the 18th of April --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are trying to say after Zivko Totic's arrest and after the attack on the Croats of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. From those days and also after the crime in Dusina, because that is when there was a general lack of security, and people started seeking ways and means of leaving Zenica. However, from the 15th hardly anyone could get out. The city was sealed off after the 15th. There were no ways of getting out. After the 18th, I already said, I already said this, after the 18th assistance was offered by Muslim citizens. They said they would take us to Zepce or Vares, not only me but to other people from town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say to area that was under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could one get out of Zenica and go to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: With great difficulty. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many Croats there were in the 1990 census in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: The 1990 census showed that there were 17 per cent of Croats, 11 per cent of Serbs, 2 or 3 per cent were others, and the remaining population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tolic, that's what you told me in response to my previous question, but could you give me the actual numbers and could you also tell me how many Croats moved out of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: During the census of 1990, it was believed that there were between 25.000 and 28.000 Croats in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about today, how many remain until the present day?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, no one knows the exact number, but people say there's not more than 5.000 or 6.000 left. And most of them left the town of Zenica after the cease-fire, after 1994, because from 1993, from the 18th of April until 1994, until the cease-fire was signed, Zenica was a big concentration camp. No one was allowed to leave Zenica. Or they could leave but with great difficulty or they would get killed as they were trying to leave it. So most people left Zenica in 1994, after the Dayton Accords were signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the Dayton Accords were signed, why did so many Croats leave Zenica? Do you have any arguments for this or do you know why this was the case?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I can tell you what I think. 1993 was a terrible year in Zenica. It was a year of famine. It was a year of persecution of Croats in Zenica. I can say that after 1994, after the cease-fire agreement was signed, it was not only the Croats who were leaving Zenica. Muslims were leaving it too, because a large number of refugees arrived in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, what are the other reasons why Croats left Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, because they were the minority people. The Muslims showed, by their attack and their behaviour, that we could not live and work there freely. I think that those are the most important reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this period, and especially on the 18th and after that, and also before that, were there any killings of Croats in Zenica, and also around Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: As regards the events that took place before Dusina and before Busovaca and before the 18th of April, I do not know. I do not know whether there were any killings. But as regards the killings that took place during the attack on the 18th of April, I can say what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us a few cases.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: The first person killed was Vlado Lovrenovic, as I said already. And he was brought to me in the early morning hours. And also in the village of Kozarci, two old men were killed. Those are my mother's uncles. One was 90 years old and the other one was 92 years old. One of them was blind and bedridden and the other one was very ill. Ivan Vidovic Ivan and Antan Vidovic were their names. Also in this village of Kozarci a three-year-old child was killed and the mother was gravely wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose child was this?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: This was the child of Zeljko and Ivanka Zrnic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They are Croats, right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Further on in the village of Zalje, which is near Zmajevac, they killed Stipo Trogrlic. Stipo Trogrlic. In this same village they also killed a child of Ana and Zejnil Pranjic. That child was one of two twins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if you refer to Gornja Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I heard that they found four burned corpses in Gornja Zenica, and one of them was the body of Stipo Kristo's father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about all of these things, were they supposed to intimidate the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: By that time ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this cause fear amongst the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, these murders happened during the attack on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall repeat my question. Did this affect the feelings of Croats, and also did this make them move out of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Indeed so. There was an attack. They killed people. They killed our relatives, our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in fear of their own lives?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we mentioned the persons who were killed, were there any people who were missing?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I heard about this. Zdeno Dujic was missing. He is the husband of an acquaintance of mine. He worked in the civilian police force in the town of Zenica. They came into his home, and they told him that he was supposed to go on assignment. He was taken away, and he was never found again. No one knows whether he is dead or alive. Also, a young boy, 17 or 18 years old, was also missing. He's also from my village, the village of Podbrezje. His name was Vjekoslav Pandza. Until this day, no one knows a thing about him. I know of another case too related to the hospital in Zenica where Dr. Sladojevic worked. He was head of the eye department. In the morning at work, they would have staff meetings of the doctors, and he protested, and he said, "Where did the people who were admitted the previous day disappear to?" So he would come into work one day, and the next day, these people would be missing. Soon after that, they came to see him at his home, they took him away, and nothing is known about him until this very day, and this was the case of Dr. Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: He was an eye doctor, a specialist, and he was also head of the department, the eye department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned Anto Dujic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is that person? Is he also missing?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he work?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: He worked in the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the civilian police. How did he disappear, now that you mentioned it?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I heard from his wife, they came to his home, they took him away, and nothing is known until the present day as to what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that I omitted a question. How many Croats live in Zenica now, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She gave the answer to that, 5.000 to 6.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All right. I apologise. I simply forgot that right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we're talking about Zenica, where were the Mujahedin staying?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: The Mujahedin were staying somewhere near the centre of town, the music school. They also were staying in a far away village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned the music school, but in addition to the music school, were they located anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: In a far away village out of town. The village was called Arnauti.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Mujahedin were in Zenica, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: That, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us an estimate?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see them often in town?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we would see them everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the villages? What about the villages around Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I can only talk about my own village where I was, Podbrezje. In Podbrezje, there was a Croat population, and in Tetovo, there was a Muslim population too, and they were in that part too because that is where they came to say in the empty houses that belonged to Serbs or -- well, that's where they lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the Croats take all of this before the 18th and after the 18th? Now we have come to the area of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: In Zenica, there were quite a few humanitarian organisations. The Muslims, to the best of my knowledge, had two such organisations, Merhamet and Agasa. The Serbs had one called Dobrotvor, and if the Croatian church, there was Caritas, the International Red Cross. Those were the humanitarian organisations that I'm aware of, and I also know that Caritas distributed aid to all the citizens of Zenica, whoever came to see them, and I'm not familiar with what others did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Croats receive humanitarian aid from Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or from Agasa, as you said? That is another Muslim humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the 18th, before the attack on places that had predominantly Croat populations and afterwards, you said that at one point in time Zenica was sealed off. What period does this blockade refer to?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: The blockade of the town of Zenica refers to the following period -- actually, it started on the 15th of April. After the 18th of April, it was intensified, so it was difficult to leave town or to enter town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could ordinary civilians leave town?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, it was difficult to get out. Ordinary civilians could not leave Zenica at all, unless they had some Muslim friends who would bring them to a point, to a checkpoint, where they would let them pass through, but that was not a sure way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We just have one more question. You mentioned the Territorial Defence. Where was the Territorial Defence located and, after that, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was at the building at Bilmiste. This was the former Yugoslav People's Army barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the authorities in Zenica carry out mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did carry out mobilisation and at work places at that. The employees of Zenica steelworks got their war assignments, their military assignments, at work, that is to say, people went to work, and they would get their war assignments, and they were taken away from work to the barracks at Bilmiste.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long would they stay there?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends. It depends on these military actions. They would spend at least a week there, and then they would go home for awhile, and then they would go back and spend another week, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any punishment in case someone did not respond to call-ups, to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: I think that, at that time, there was not a single person who would not have responded. I'm not aware of this, but most people joined the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who went to the Territorial Defence? You said it was the employed persons who went.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Everyone went, almost everyone, almost all citizens of Zenica, men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say military-aged men?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, have I no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we adjourn, could I know if there will be any cross-examination by other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witnesses will be questioned by Ranko Radovic and Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until tomorrow at 1.30. Tomorrow we will be sitting -- yes, Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Counsel Susak, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I suggest that two documents be admitted into evidence, that is to say, the decision on custody and the decision on release from custody for this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We only received one decision, the one for the release. The other one was never handed to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I have both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But we don't have it. D8/4 is the only one we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, but I have extra copies, and I shall submit this other document to you forthwith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but then we must give time to the Prosecution to consider those and see whether they have any objections. So you can hand in now this document, and tomorrow we will decide whether or not both documents are admitted into evidence. As I say, tomorrow, we will be sitting from 1.30 until 6.00 p.m. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
